questions.q: What problem does the lesson describe with running Entra ID for Azure and a completely separate set of AWS IAM users/keys for AWS?
options: AWS does not support any form of external identity federation
Disabling a user in Entra ID has no effect on their separate AWS access keys, so a departed employee can retain AWS access for weeks
Conditional Access policies automatically apply to AWS without any configuration
Azure RBAC and AWS IAM use an identical permission model by default
questions.explain: Two unconnected identity stores mean an action in one (disabling a user in Entra ID) doesn't propagate to the other, leaving a departed employee's AWS access keys working until someone manually revokes them.

questions.q: How does AWS IAM Identity Center let a user sign in without a separate AWS username and password?
options: It federates authentication to an external identity provider like Microsoft Entra ID over SAML, mapping the authenticated identity to permission sets
It automatically imports Active Directory passwords into AWS Secrets Manager
It requires every user to create an AWS root account first
It disables MFA to simplify the sign-in flow
questions.explain: IAM Identity Center (the successor to AWS SSO) federates sign-in over SAML, so the user authenticates through Entra ID and is mapped to permission sets in the target AWS account.

questions.q: Why does a user's Conditional Access policy — including device compliance and risk evaluation — still apply when they access AWS through the federated IAM Identity Center path?
options: Because AWS re-implements Conditional Access natively inside IAM Identity Center
Because Conditional Access policies are copied manually into every AWS account
Because the sign-in still goes through Microsoft Entra ID, which evaluates the same policy regardless of which downstream system the user is ultimately reaching
It does not apply; AWS access is entirely outside Conditional Access's reach
questions.explain: Because the federated sign-in is authenticated by Entra ID, it passes through the same Conditional Access evaluation as any other app — device compliance, risk, and continuous access evaluation included.

questions.q: How does the lesson describe the relationship between Azure PIM's eligible/activate/time-boxed model and AWS STS-issued temporary credentials?
options: They are unrelated mechanisms that happen to share no design similarities
AWS STS replaces the need for PIM entirely once federation is configured
PIM only applies to read-only roles, while STS only applies to administrative roles
They express the same underlying principle — privilege borrowed for a bounded, expiring window rather than held indefinitely — in two different clouds
questions.explain: PIM's eligible-then-activated-then-time-boxed pattern and STS's temporary, expiring credentials tied to an assumed role are the same design philosophy implemented separately in Azure and AWS.

questions.q: What is the point of tracing a single access request end to end through this identity fabric, according to the lesson's closing framing?
options: To confirm that all three components — Entra ID, Conditional Access, and AWS IAM roles — have identical user interfaces
To show there is no silent gap where a disabled account, non-compliant device, or expired elevation could still reach a resource, in either cloud
To justify removing Conditional Access once PIM and STS are in place
To determine which cloud provider is cheaper to operate
questions.explain: A capstone-level architecture review isn't about naming the pieces — it's about verifying that identity, device, risk, and time-boxed elevation are checked at every point along the path, with no gap in either cloud.
